items.title: The d'Alembert and vakonomic motions of $z'=xy'$ differ from the same initial data
items.design_state: completed-local-counterexample; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
Every d'Alembert motion of the constraint $z'=xy'$ with unit mass and zero applied force that
satisfies the initial data

$$(x,y,z)(0)=(0,0,0),\qquad(x',y',z')(0)=(1,1,0)$$

is a vakonomic motion of the same constraint with the same initial data.
items.strategy: Solve the d'Alembert equations explicitly for the given data; assume the vakonomic system with the same data and derive eta=0, contradicting the explicit d'Alembert acceleration.

items.title: Conserved charges for translation, rotation and boost symmetries of a mechanical Lagrangian
items.design_state: completed-local-corollary; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $m>0$, let $a_0<b_0$ be reals, let $\varepsilon>0$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and nonempty, let
$U_0:(a_0-\varepsilon,b_0+\varepsilon)\times U\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$, and let

$$\mathcal L(t,q,v):=\tfrac12m|v|^2-U_0(t,q)$$

be the corresponding Lagrangian chart ([[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Let $q:I\to U$ be a $C^2$ Euler–Lagrange solution on an open
interval $[a_0,b_0]\subseteq I\subseteq(a_0-\varepsilon,b_0+\varepsilon)$. Then:

1. **(translation)** if $a\in\mathbb R^n$ and $a\cdot\nabla_qU_0(t,q)=0$ for every $(t,q)$, then
   $P_a(t):=m\,a\cdot q'(t)$ is constant on $I$;
2. **(rotation)** if $n=3$, $a\in\mathbb R^3$ and $(a\times q)\cdot\nabla U_0(t,q)=0$ for every
   $(t,q)$, then $J_a(t):=m\,(q(t)\times q'(t))\cdot a$ is constant on $I$;
3. **(boost)** if $a\in\mathbb R^n$ and $a\cdot\nabla_qU_0=0$ on the whole chart, then
   $K_a(t):=a\cdot\bigl(t\,m\,q'(t)-m\,q(t)\bigr)$ is constant on $I$.
items.strategy: Apply the general symmetry identity to the specific generators and solve for the conserved charge in each case.

D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge Part II Mathematical Tripos), Section 2.4.1 (the translation and rotation charges) and Section 1.2 (the Galilean group and boosts), printed pages 23-26 and 2-5

items.title: Reduced d'Alembert equation for an immersion: generalized forces and the quadratic correction
items.design_state: completed-local-corollary; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
Let $n,m\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and nonempty, and let
$X:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ be of class $C^3$ with $DX(q)$ injective for every $q\in\Omega$; fix an
immersion in the sense of [[def-euclidean-submersions-and-immersions]] (this forces $n\le m$).
Let $M\in M_m(\mathbb R)$ be symmetric positive definite, meaning $M^{\mathsf T}=M$ and $u^{\mathsf T}Mu>0$ for every $0\ne u\in\mathbb R^m$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $F:D\to\mathbb R^m$ be continuous, let
$I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval ([[def-interval]]), and let
$q:I\to\Omega$ be a $C^2$ curve with $x(t):=X(q(t))$ and $(t,x(t),x'(t))\in D$ for all $t\in I$. Suppose there is a continuous
$R:I\to\mathbb R^m$ with

$$Mx''(t)=F\bigl(t,x(t),x'(t)\bigr)+R(t),\qquad R(t)\cdot DX(q(t))\delta=0\quad\text{for all }\delta\in\mathbb R^n,\ t\in I .$$

Then, writing $DX(q(t))^{\mathsf T}$ for the transpose and
$\bigl(X_{qq}[q',q']\bigr)_k:=\sum_{i,j}\partial_i\partial_jX_k(q)q_i'q_j'$, one has

$$DX(q)^{\mathsf T}MDX(q)\,q''=DX(q)^{\mathsf T}F(t,x,x')-DX(q)^{\mathsf T}M\,X_{qq}[q',q']$$

on $I$. The vector $DX(q)^{\mathsf T}F(t,x,x')$ is the **generalized force** of the ambient force
$F$ in the coordinates $q$, and $DX^{\mathsf T}M X_{qq}[q',q']$ is the acceleration correction of
the parametrisation; when $X$ is affine, the correction vanishes.
items.strategy: Pull the ambient equation back by DX^T; the ideal reaction drops out and the second-derivative chain rule produces the parametrisation correction.

references.title: D. Cline, Variational Principles in Classical Mechanics (2nd edition, University of Rochester River Campus Libraries, open textbook, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), Section 6.3 (Lagrange Equations from d'Alembert's Principle: generalized coordinates and generalized forces)

D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge Part II Mathematical Tripos), Section 2.3 'Constraints and Generalised Coordinates' (constraint forces and the elimination of constraints by generalised coordinates), printed pages 17-22

items.title: A regular holonomic constraint, its virtual displacements and the ideal-reaction law
items.design_state: completed-local-definition; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$ and $k\ge1$, let $O\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open and nonempty, let
$G:O\to\mathbb R^k$ be of class $C^2$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and write $G_q(t,q)$ for the Jacobian matrix of
$q\mapsto G(t,q)$ ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]), a $k\times n$ matrix. The constraint

$$G(t,q)=0$$

is **regular** when

$$G_q(t,q)\ \text{has rank }k\ \text{for every }(t,q)\in O,$$

equivalently when $G_q$ is surjective at every point ([[def-euclidean-submersions-and-immersions]]).
Under this hypothesis each fibre $G(t,\cdot)^{-1}(0)$ is a regular level set and every point of it
is a regular point in the sense of [[def-regular-critical-points-values-and-level-sets]].

**Constraint set and admissible data.** Fix a symmetric positive definite matrix
$M\in M_n(\mathbb R)$, meaning $M^{\mathsf T}=M$ and $u^{\mathsf T}Mu>0$ for every $0\ne u\in\mathbb R^n$, and a continuous map
$f:O\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$, the **given force**. A map $q:I\to\mathbb R^n$ on an open
interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) is a **constrained curve** when

$$(t,q(t))\in O,\qquad G\bigl(t,q(t)\bigr)=0\qquad(t\in I).$$

**Virtual displacements and permitted velocities.** For $(t,q)\in O$ the **virtual displacements**
at $(t,q)$ are the elements of the kernel

$$V(t,q):=\ker G_q(t,q)=\bigl\{\delta\in\mathbb R^n:G_q(t,q)\delta=0\bigr\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n,$$

the tangent space to the level set of $G(t,\cdot)$ at $q$ in the sense of
[[def-tangent-space-to-a-regular-level-set]]; a **permitted velocity** at $(t,q)$ is a vector
$v\in\mathbb R^n$ with

$$G_t(t,q)+G_q(t,q)v=0 .$$

For a $C^1$ constrained curve the differentiated constraint forces
$G_t(t,q(t))+G_q(t,q(t))q'(t)=0$, so its velocity is automatically permitted; the permitted
condition is stated separately because it is the correct initial condition for the first-order
system below.

**Ideal-constraint motions.** A $C^2$ constrained curve $q:I\to\mathbb R^n$ is an
**ideal-constraint motion** of the data $(G,M,f)$ when

1. $q'(t)$ is a permitted velocity at $(t,q(t))$ for every $t\in I$, and
2. there is a continuous map $\lambda:I\to\mathbb R^k$ with

$$Mq''(t)=f\bigl(t,q(t),q'(t)\bigr)+G_q\bigl(t,q(t)\bigr)^{\mathsf T}\lambda(t)\qquad(t\in I).$$

The vector field $R(t):=Mq''(t)-f(t,q(t),q'(t))$ is the **reaction** and
$R=G_q^{\mathsf T}\lambda$ is its **multiplier form**. Since
$G_q(t,q)^{\mathsf T}\lambda\cdot\delta=\lambda\cdot G_q(t,q)\delta=0$ for every
$\delta\in V(t,q)$, every ideal-constraint motion satisfies the **d'Alembert condition**

$$\bigl(Mq''(t)-f(t,q(t),q'(t))\bigr)\cdot\delta=0\qquad\text{for every }\delta\in V(t,q(t)),$$

i.e. the reaction performs no virtual work; the converse implication, that every curve satisfying
the d'Alembert condition is an ideal-constraint motion with a *unique* multiplier, together with
uniqueness of the resulting acceleration, is the content of
[[lem-cm-constraint-multipliers-and-accelerations]] and is not assumed here.

**Scope.** The definition is chartwise and time-dependent: the constraint may depend on $t$
(rheonomic case), its velocity condition is the fixed-time linearisation recorded above, and no
relation between the *variational* (vakonomic) treatment of the constraint and the present
d'Alembert law is asserted. The construction and long-time behaviour of solutions is the subject of
[[prop-cm-ideal-holonomic-system-in-a-time-dependent-chart]]. For a holonomic constraint written
in a chart, the multiplier $\lambda$ is not a measured quantity: only the reaction
$G_q^{\mathsf T}\lambda$ enters the equations of motion.
items.strategy: Define the regular constraint, virtual displacements, permitted velocities and the ideal-reaction law with the d'Alembert condition derived as a consequence.

items.title: Infinitesimal point symmetry of a time-dependent Lagrangian and its conserved charge
items.design_state: completed-local-definition; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
Let $(O,\mathcal L)$ be a time-dependent Lagrangian chart over $[a,b]\times U$ in the sense of
[[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]]. Let $V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $A\subseteq\mathbb R\times V$ be open sets containing respectively the configuration projection of $O$ and its time-configuration projection. Let

$$\xi:V\longrightarrow\mathbb R^n,\qquad B:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R$$

be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); write $D\xi(q)\in M_n(\mathbb R)$
for the Jacobian matrix of $\xi$ at $q$ ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]],
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]), and for a $C^1$ function $\varphi(t,q)$ write

$$D_t\varphi(t,q,v):=\varphi_t(t,q)+\varphi_q(t,q)\cdot v .$$

The pair $(\xi,B)$ is an **infinitesimal point symmetry of $\mathcal L$** when the identity

$$\mathcal L_q(t,q,v)\cdot\xi(q)+\mathcal L_v(t,q,v)\cdot D\xi(q)v =B_t(t,q)+B_q(t,q)\cdot v$$

holds for every $(t,q,v)\in O$. The **charge of the pair** is the function

$$C(t,q,v):=\mathcal L_v(t,q,v)\cdot\xi(q)-B(t,q).$$

**Reading of the identity.** The left-hand side is the derivative of the Lagrangian under the
infinitesimal family of point transformations

$$q\longmapsto q+s\,\xi(q),\qquad t\longmapsto t$$

with the velocity transformed accordingly by $v\mapsto v+s\,D\xi(q)v$, and the right-hand side is
the total derivative $\frac{d}{dt}B(t,q(t))$ along a $C^1$ trajectory with $q'(t)=v$; thus the identity says that the infinitesimal variation of
$\mathcal L$ is a total time derivative of the chart function $B$. In particular:

- Taking $B=0$ reduces the identity to
  $\mathcal L_q(t,q,v)\cdot\xi(q)+\mathcal L_v(t,q,v)\cdot D\xi(q)v=0$, the invariance of
  $\mathcal L$ under the infinitesimal family.
- For a constant field $\xi\equiv a$ one has $D\xi=0$, and the identity reads
  $\mathcal L_q\cdot a=B_t+B_q\cdot v$; when $B$ is independent of $q$ this is the statement that
  $\mathcal L$ is unchanged by the translation $q\mapsto q+sa$ up to a total time derivative.

**Scope.** The definition is an identity imposed on the chart data; it does not assert that a
given Lagrangian possesses any symmetry, nor that a symmetry of the configuration space, a frame
change or any kinematic structure automatically induces one. Whether a symmetry produces a
conserved quantity along the Euler–Lagrange solutions is the theorem
[[thm-cm-point-symmetry-charge-is-conserved]]; the general reparametrisation version is
[[thm-cm-point-noether-identity-with-time-reparametrization]], and the scope of the statement for
physical models is recorded in [[rem-cm-scope-of-point-symmetry]].
items.strategy: Define the symmetry data, the identity and the charge, distinguishing the time-independent case; the conservation theorem is separately stated.

D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge Part II Mathematical Tripos), Section 2.4.1 'Noether's Theorem' (continuous symmetries of the Lagrangian), printed pages 24-26

items.title: The Legendre map of a time-dependent Lagrangian: regularity and hyperregularity
items.design_state: completed-local-definition; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
**Chart data.** Let $n\ge1$, let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ and $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and
nonempty, and let

$$\mathcal L:J\times U\times\mathbb R^n\longrightarrow\mathbb R$$

be of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Such a map is a **fibre-full
time-dependent Lagrangian chart**; it is the special case of the chart of
[[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]] in which the velocity block is the whole space
$\mathbb R^n$ at every $(t,q)\in J\times U$. Write $\mathcal L_v(t,q,v)\in\mathbb R^n$ for the
Euclidean gradient of $\mathcal L$ in its third slot and $\mathcal L_{vv}(t,q,v)\in M_n(\mathbb R)$
for the matrix of second partial derivatives in the third slot
([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]).

**Legendre map.** The **Legendre map** of $\mathcal L$ is the map

$$\mathbb F_{\mathcal L}:J\times U\times\mathbb R^n\longrightarrow J\times U\times\mathbb R^n, \qquad \mathbb F_{\mathcal L}(t,q,v):=\bigl(t,q,\mathcal L_v(t,q,v)\bigr).$$

The fibre coordinate of the target is called the **momentum** and is written
$p:=\mathcal L_v(t,q,v)$. Thus $\mathbb F_{\mathcal L}$ is the identity in the first two slots and
the gradient in the velocity slot. Since $\mathcal L$ is $C^2$, $\mathbb F_{\mathcal L}$ is $C^1$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

**Regularity.** Let $(t,q,v)\in J\times U\times\mathbb R^n$. The Legendre map is **regular at
$(t,q,v)$** when the velocity Hessian is nonsingular,

$$\det\mathcal L_{vv}(t,q,v)\ne0 ;$$

it is **regular (on the chart)** when it is regular at every point. At fixed $(t,q)$ this is
exactly the condition under which the map $v\mapsto(q,\mathcal L_v(t,q,v))$ is locally invertible
near $v$, a statement made precise and proved in
[[lem-cm-legendre-map-local-invertibility]].

**Hyperregularity.** The Lagrangian $\mathcal L$ is **hyperregular (on the chart)** when for every
$(t,q)\in J\times U$ the map

$$v\longmapsto\mathcal L_v(t,q,v)$$

is a bijection of $\mathbb R^n$ onto $\mathbb R^n$ and the inverse assignment

$$(t,q,p)\longmapsto v(t,q,p),\qquad \mathcal L_v\bigl(t,q,v(t,q,p)\bigr)=p,$$

is defined on all of $J\times U\times\mathbb R^n$ and is of class $C^1$. In that case $v$ is called
the **inverse Legendre branch** of $\mathcal L$, and the **Hamiltonian of the branch** is

$$H:J\times U\times\mathbb R^n\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad H(t,q,p):=p\cdot v(t,q,p)-\mathcal L\bigl(t,q,v(t,q,p)\bigr).$$

The Hamiltonian is $C^1$ on its domain, being a sum of products of $C^1$ maps.

The definition asserts nothing about solving the equations of motion: the equivalence of the
Euler–Lagrange equation with Hamilton's equations on an inverse branch, and the differential of
$H$, are proved in [[prop-cm-hamiltonian-branch-identities]].
items.strategy: Define the fibre-full chart, the Legendre map, regularity, hyperregularity, the inverse branch and the Hamiltonian with all regularity hypotheses explicit.

D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge Part II Mathematical Tripos), Section 4.1.1 'The Legendre Transform' (the transform from L to H and the convexity requirement), printed pages 82-83

items.title: The velocity constraint $z'=xy'$: virtual displacements, the d'Alembert law and the vakonomic law
items.design_state: completed-local-definition; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
Work in $\mathbb R^3$ with coordinates $(x,y,z)$ on configuration space and velocities
$(x',y',z')$; inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. All intervals
below are open intervals of $\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]), and a map on an interval is said to be
$C^r$ when all its components are ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

**The constraint and its virtual displacements.** The **constraint law** is

$$z'=xy' .$$

A configuration $q=(x,y,z)$ is written without a subscript, and its velocity is
$v=(x',y',z')$. The **allowed velocities** at $q$ and the **virtual displacements** at $q$ are
both the same linear subspace

$$D(q):=\bigl\{w=(w_x,w_y,w_z)\in\mathbb R^3:w_z=xw_y\bigr\}=\operatorname{span}\bigl\{(1,0,0),(0,1,x)\bigr\}\subseteq\mathbb R^3 .$$

Thus a virtual displacement $\delta=(\delta x,\delta y,\delta z)$ obeys $\delta z=x\,\delta y$;
this is the Chetaev prescription for the linear velocity constraint $z'-xy'=0$, in which the
virtual displacements are computed from the constraint function frozen at the current
configuration.

**Sample Lagrangian and zero applied force.** The adopted Lagrangian is

$$L_0(q,v):=\tfrac12|v|^2=\tfrac12\bigl(x'^2+y'^2+z'^2\bigr),$$

of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3$; no applied force is introduced. Since
$L_0$ is a special case of a Lagrangian chart as in [[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]]
(with $n=3$, $U=\mathbb R^3$ and $O=\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3$), the words
stationary, action and Euler--Lagrange expression below have the meanings fixed there whenever
they are used.

**d'Alembert motions.** A $C^2$ curve $q:I\to\mathbb R^3$ is a **d'Alembert motion** of the
constraint $z'=xy'$ when

1. $z'(t)=x(t)y'(t)$ for every $t\in I$, and
2. $q''(t)\cdot\delta=0$ for every $\delta\in D(q(t))$ and every $t\in I$.

Clause 2 is the ideal-reaction (d'Alembert) condition for unit mass and zero applied force:
the acceleration has no component along any admissible virtual displacement, so the constraint
force performs no virtual work.

**The augmented functional and the vakonomic law.** Let $a<b$ be reals with $[a,b]\subseteq I_0$
for some open interval $I_0$. For a $C^2$ curve $q:I_0\to\mathbb R^3$ and a $C^2$ function
$\eta:I_0\to\mathbb R$ put

$$\Phi(q,\eta):=\int_a^b\Bigl[\tfrac12|q'(t)|^2+\eta(t)\bigl(z'(t)-x(t)y'(t)\bigr)\Bigr]dt .$$

The integrand is continuous because $q,q'$ and $\eta$ are continuous, so $\Phi(q,\eta)$ is a
well-defined real number ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]],
[[def-darboux-integral]], [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]). An **admissible pair
variation** of a pair $(q,\eta)$ is a pair of $C^2$ maps $(\xi,\zeta)$ on $I_0$ with
$\xi(a)=\xi(b)=0$, and the pair $(q,\eta)$ is a **vakonomic stationary pair** when the
ordinary two-sided directional derivative

$$\frac{d}{ds}\Big|_{s=0}\Phi(q+s\xi,\eta+s\zeta)$$

exists and equals $0$ for every admissible pair variation $(\xi,\zeta)$ with
$\xi(a)=\xi(b)=0$. A $C^2$ curve $q:I_0\to\mathbb R^3$ is a **vakonomic motion** of the
constraint when there is a $C^2$ function $\eta$ on $I_0$ such that $(q,\eta)$ is a vakonomic
stationary pair on some $[a,b]\subseteq I_0$ with $a<b$.

**Scope.** Both laws are *prescriptions* for the same constraint, and the definition deliberately
does not identify them: the d'Alembert law is a differential condition on the acceleration along
the constraint distribution, while the vakonomic law arises from stationarity of the augmented
functional over curves and multipliers. For this constraint the two prescriptions give different
motions from the same initial data; that is the content of
[[cex-cm-dalembert-and-vakonomic-evolutions-differ]]. The constraint law $z'=xy'$ is not
equivalent to any condition $G(q)=\text{const}$ for a $C^2$ function $G$ with nonvanishing
differential, as proved in [[prop-cm-nonholonomic-distribution-is-not-tangent-to-level-sets]];
this is the sense in which the constraint is non-holonomic.
items.strategy: Define the distribution of allowed displacements and the d'Alembert and vakonomic laws as separate models; non-integrability and the difference are proved in the two companion items.

items.title: A time-dependent Lagrangian chart, its action functional and its fixed-endpoint first variations
items.design_state: completed-local-definition; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
**Chart data.** Let $n\ge1$, let $a<b$ be reals and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and
nonempty. Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n$ be an open set with

$$[a,b]\times U\times\mathbb R^n\subseteq O,$$

and let $\mathcal L:O\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). The pair $(O,\mathcal L)$ is a **time-dependent
Lagrangian chart over $[a,b]\times U$**. The three slots of $\mathcal L$ are written
$(t,q,v)$, so that $t$ is the time, $q$ the configuration and $v$ the velocity; the open set
$O$ has the three coordinate blocks of sizes $1,n,n$.

**Admissible curves and variations.** A map $q:[a,b]\to U$ is **of class $C^2$** when there are
$\varepsilon>0$ and a $C^2$ map $\tilde q:(a-\varepsilon,b+\varepsilon)\to\mathbb R^n$ with
$\tilde q|_{[a,b]}=q$ and $\tilde q(t)\in U$ for every $t\in[a,b]$; the derivative $q'$ and the
second derivative $q''$ below are those of any such extension, and they are independent of the
extension on $[a,b]$. A **variation** of a $C^2$ curve $q$ is a map $\eta:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n$ of
class $C^2$ in the same sense with

$$\eta(a)=\eta(b)=0 .$$

Thus the admissible curves and variations are the restrictions to $[a,b]$ of $C^2$ maps on a
common open interval, exactly the convention under which $C^2$ data on a closed interval are used
in [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]] and in the classical treatments cited
below.

**The action.** For a $C^2$ curve $q:[a,b]\to U$ the map $t\mapsto\mathcal L(t,q(t),q'(t))$ is
continuous on $[a,b]$, because $q,q'$ are continuous and $\mathcal L$ is continuous
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]); it is therefore Darboux integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). The **action** of $q$ is the real number

$$S(q):=\int_a^b\mathcal L\bigl(t,q(t),q'(t)\bigr)\,dt .$$

**First variation.** For a $C^2$ curve $q$ and a variation $\eta$ the curve $q_\varepsilon:=q+\varepsilon\eta$
takes values in $U$ for all sufficiently small $|\varepsilon|$; this is proved in
[[lem-cm-first-variation-formula]] and is *not* part of the present definition. The **first
variation of $S$ at $q$ in the direction $\eta$** is the ordinary two-sided derivative at $\varepsilon=0$
of the function $\varepsilon\mapsto S(q+\varepsilon\eta)$, written

$$\delta S(q)[\eta]:=\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\Big|_{\varepsilon=0}S(q+\varepsilon\eta),$$

whenever this derivative exists; [[lem-cm-first-variation-formula]] proves that it does exist
under the present hypotheses and computes it, so the notation denotes a single real number for
every pair $(q,\eta)$ arising here.

**Euler–Lagrange expression.** Let $\mathcal L_q(t,q,v)\in\mathbb R^n$ and
$\mathcal L_v(t,q,v)\in\mathbb R^n$ be the gradients of $\mathcal L$ in the second and third slots
([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]). Since
$\mathcal L$ is $C^2$, the maps $t\mapsto\mathcal L_v(t,q(t),q'(t))$ are $C^1$ and
$t\mapsto\mathcal L_q(t,q(t),q'(t))$ is continuous on $[a,b]$. The **Euler–Lagrange expression of
$\mathcal L$ along $q$** is the continuous map

$$E_{\mathcal L}(q)(t):=\mathcal L_q\bigl(t,q(t),q'(t)\bigr)-\frac{d}{dt}\Bigl(\mathcal L_v\bigl(t,q(t),q'(t)\bigr)\Bigr)\in\mathbb R^n.$$

**Stationarity.** A $C^2$ curve $q$ is **stationary for $S$** when

$$\delta S(q)[\eta]=0\qquad\text{for every variation }\eta.$$

**Scope.** The definition introduces only chart data, the action and its first variation. It
asserts nothing about minimising $S$, nothing about the existence of stationary curves and nothing
about any physical interpretation of $\mathcal L$; the equivalence of stationarity with the
vanishing of $E_{\mathcal L}(q)$ is the theorem [[thm-cm-stationarity-iff-euler-lagrange]], and
the distinction between stationary and minimising curves is recorded in
[[rem-cm-scope-of-stationarity]].
items.strategy: Define the chart, action and first variation with explicit regularity and extension conventions; the existence of the first variation is contracted to lem-cm-first-variation-formula (justified_by), and no solvability or minimisation is assumed.

items.design_state: completed-local-lemma; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:

$\beta_{c,r}:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ by

$$\beta_{c,r}(t):=h\bigl(1-\tfrac{|t-c|}{r}\bigr)\ \text{for }|t-c|<r,\qquad \beta_{c,r}(t):=0\ \text{for }|t-c|\ge r .$$

Then:

1. $h(0)=0$, $h(1)=1$, $h'(0)=h'(1)=0$, $h''(0)=h''(1)=0$, and $0\le h\le1$ on $[0,1]$ with
   $h(s)>0$ for $0<s<1$;
2. $\beta_{c,r}$ is of class $C^2$ on $\mathbb R$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]),
   $0\le\beta_{c,r}\le1$, $\beta_{c,r}(c)=1$, $\beta_{c,r}(t)>0$ for $|t-c|<r$, and
   $\beta_{c,r}(t)=0$ for $|t-c|\ge r$;
3. **(detection)** let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $E:J\to\mathbb R$ be
   continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]) and let $t_0\in J$ with $E(t_0)\ne0$. Then there is
   $\rho>0$ with $[t_0-\rho,t_0+\rho]\subseteq J$ such that, with $\beta:=\beta_{t_0,\rho}$,

$$\int_{t_0-\rho}^{t_0+\rho}E(t)\beta(t)\,dt\ne0 .$$

**Conventions.** The displayed integral is the Darboux integral over the closed bounded interval
$[t_0-\rho,t_0+\rho]$ of the continuous function $t\mapsto E(t)\beta(t)$
([[def-darboux-integral]], [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]); note that $\beta$ vanishes
at both endpoints and outside the interval, so no extension convention is needed.

([[def-cm-legendre-map-in-a-time-dependent-chart]]). Then:

   $(t,q,v)$ in the sense of [[def-cm-legendre-map-in-a-time-dependent-chart]] exactly when its
   derivative there is invertible;

   $C^1$ diffeomorphism at $(t_0,q_0,v_0)$: there are open neighbourhoods
   $W\ni(t_0,q_0,v_0)$ and $W'\ni\mathbb F_{\mathcal L}(t_0,q_0,v_0)$ such that

items.title: Coordinate covariance of the Euler-Lagrange expression under time-dependent point transformations
items.design_state: completed-local-proposition; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open and nonempty, and let
$X:\Omega\to\mathbb R^n$ be of class $C^3$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) with
$X_q(t,q)$ invertible for every $(t,q)\in\Omega$
([[def-invertible-euclidean-linear-map]], [[def-linear-map]]). Let $O_x\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n$
be open and let $L:O_x\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$. Put

$$O:=\bigl\{(t,q,v)\in\Omega\times\mathbb R^n:\bigl(t,X(t,q),X_t(t,q)+X_q(t,q)v\bigr)\in O_x\bigr\},\qquad \widetilde L(t,q,v):=L\bigl(t,X(t,q),X_t(t,q)+X_q(t,q)v\bigr).$$

Then:

1. $O$ is open, $O\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n$, and $\widetilde L$ is of
   class $C^2$ on $O$;
2. with $w:=X_t(t,q)+X_q(t,q)v$ one has
   $\widetilde L_v(t,q,v)=X_q(t,q)^{\mathsf T}L_v(t,X(t,q),w)$;
3. $\widetilde L_q(t,q,v)=X_q^{\mathsf T}L_x+\bigl(X_{tq}+X_{qq}[v]\bigr)^{\mathsf T}L_v$, where
   $X_{tq}$ is the $t$-derivative of $X_q$ and $X_{qq}[v]$ is the matrix with entries
   $\sum_j\partial_j\partial_iX_k(t,q)v_j$, all evaluated at $(t,q)$ and $L_x,L_v$ at
   $(t,X(t,q),w)$;
4. **(transport)** let $a<b$ be reals and let $q:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n$ be a $C^2$ curve with
   $(t,q(t),q'(t))\in O$ for all $t\in[a,b]$, put $x(t):=X(t,q(t))$, and define
   $P(t):=\widetilde L_v(t,q(t),q'(t))$ and $p(t):=L_v(t,x(t),x'(t))$, which are $C^1$. Then

$$\frac{d}{dt}P(t)-\widetilde L_q\bigl(t,q(t),q'(t)\bigr) =X_q\bigl(t,q(t)\bigr)^{\mathsf T}\Bigl(\frac{d}{dt}p(t)-L_x\bigl(t,x(t),x'(t)\bigr)\Bigr) \qquad(t\in[a,b]);$$

   consequently, since $X_q(t,q(t))$ is invertible, the Euler–Lagrange expression of
   $\widetilde L$ vanishes along $q$ if and only if the Euler–Lagrange expression of $L$ vanishes
   along $x$.
items.strategy: Chain rule and mixed-partial equality for the chart change; invertibility of X_q for the equivalence; project the ambient equation for the reduced form.

items.design_state: completed-local-proposition; recorded in the batch notes

Lagrangian chart that is hyperregular, with inverse Legendre branch $v(t,q,p)$ and Hamiltonian
$H(t,q,p)=p\cdot v(t,q,p)-\mathcal L(t,q,v(t,q,p))$
([[def-cm-legendre-map-in-a-time-dependent-chart]]). Then:

1. **(differential)** for every $(t,q,p)\in J\times U\times\mathbb R^n$,

$$H_p(t,q,p)=v(t,q,p),\qquad H_q(t,q,p)=-\mathcal L_q\bigl(t,q,v(t,q,p)\bigr),\qquad H_t(t,q,p)=-\mathcal L_t\bigl(t,q,v(t,q,p)\bigr);$$

2. **(equivalence)** for a $C^1$ curve $(q,p):I\to U\times\mathbb R^n$ on an open interval $I\subseteq J$
   ([[def-interval]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]) the following are
   equivalent:
   (a) $q$ is $C^2$ and $E_{\mathcal L}(q)(t)=0$ for all $t\in I$, with
   $p(t)=\mathcal L_v\bigl(t,q(t),q'(t)\bigr)$;
   (b) $(q,p)$ satisfies Hamilton's equations
   $q'(t)=H_p\bigl(t,q(t),p(t)\bigr)$ and $p'(t)=-H_q\bigl(t,q(t),p(t)\bigr)$ for all $t\in I$;
3. **(energy)** along any curve satisfying (a) or (b), the function
   $e(t):=\mathcal L_v(t,q,q')\cdot q'(t)-\mathcal L(t,q(t),q'(t))$ equals $H(t,q(t),p(t))$ and
   satisfies $e'(t)=-\mathcal L_t(t,q(t),q'(t))$ on $I$; in particular, if $\mathcal L_t$ vanishes
   on the set $\{(s,q(s),q'(s)):s\in I\}$, then $e$ is constant on $I$.

items.statement:
Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open and nonempty, let $G:O\to\mathbb R^k$ be of
class $C^3$ with $G_q(t,q)$ of rank $k$ for every $(t,q)\in O$ (a regular holonomic constraint,
[[def-cm-holonomic-constraint-and-ideal-reactions]]), let $M\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ be symmetric
positive definite, and let $f:O\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be of class $C^1$. Define, for
$(t,q,v)\in O\times\mathbb R^n$,

$$C(t,q):=G_q(t,q)M^{-1}G_q(t,q)^{\mathsf T},\qquad \Lambda(t,q,v):=-C(t,q)^{-1}\Bigl[G_qM^{-1}f+G_{tt}+2G_{tq}[v]+G_{qq}[v,v]\Bigr],\qquad a(t,q,v):=M^{-1}\bigl(f+G_q^{\mathsf T}\Lambda\bigr),$$

where all terms in the bracket are evaluated at $(t,q,v)$, and
$2G_{tq}[v]:=\sum_i2\partial_t\partial_{q_i}G\,v_i$ and
$G_{qq}[v,v]:=\sum_{i,j}\partial_i\partial_jG\,v_iv_j$. Then:

1. $C$ is symmetric positive definite and $C^{-1}$, $\Lambda$ and $a$ are of class $C^1$ on
   $O\times\mathbb R^n$; in particular $a$ is locally Lipschitz in $(q,v)$;
2. through every $(t_0,q_0,v_0)\in O\times\mathbb R^n$ there is a unique maximal solution
   $(q,v):I_{t_0}\to\mathbb R^{2n}$, with $(t,q(t),v(t))\in O\times\mathbb R^n$, of the first-order system

$$q'=v,\qquad v'=a(t,q,v) ;$$

3. if the data satisfy the consistency conditions

$$G(t_0,q_0)=0,\qquad G_t(t_0,q_0)+G_q(t_0,q_0)v_0=0,$$

   then the maximal solution satisfies $G(t,q(t))=0$ and
   $G_t(t,q(t))+G_q(t,q(t))q'(t)=0$ for all $t\in I_{t_0}$; consequently $q$ is an
   ideal-constraint motion of $(G,M,f)$ with multiplier $\lambda(t)=\Lambda(t,q(t),v(t))$, and
   its reaction $R=G_q^{\mathsf T}\Lambda$ satisfies the power identity

$$R(t)\cdot q'(t)=-\Lambda(t,q(t),v(t))\cdot G_t(t,q(t)) ;$$

4. conversely, every $C^2$ ideal-constraint motion $q:I\to\mathbb R^n$ of $(G,M,f)$ whose velocity
   is permitted solves this first-order system with $v=q'$; hence the ideal-constraint motions
   with permitted velocity are exactly the solutions of the system with consistent data.

$$\mathcal L(t,q,v):=\tfrac12v^{\mathsf T}G(t,q)v+A(t,q)\cdot v-V(t,q),$$

items.title: The distribution $\mathrm{span}\{\partial_x,\partial_y+x\partial_z\}$ is not tangent to any regular level sets
items.design_state: completed-local-proposition; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and nonempty, and consider the derivations
$A:=\partial_x$ and $B:=\partial_y+x\,\partial_z$ acting on $C^2$ functions on $O$. If
$G:O\to\mathbb R$ is of class $C^2$ with

$$AG=0\quad\text{and}\quad BG=0\quad\text{on }O,$$

then $DG=0$ on $O$. Consequently, if $G:O\to\mathbb R$ is $C^2$ and $DG(q)\ne0$ for every
$q\in O$ (so that every level set of $G$ is a regular level set with tangent space
$\ker DG(q)$, [[def-regular-critical-points-values-and-level-sets]],
[[def-tangent-space-to-a-regular-level-set]]), then the distribution
$D(q)=\operatorname{span}\{A(q),B(q)\}$ of [[def-cm-nonholonomic-velocity-constraint-law]] cannot equal $\ker DG(q)$ for every $q\in O$; that is, no such $G$ has level sets whose tangent planes are everywhere the
virtual displacements of the constraint $z'=xy'$.
items.strategy: Compute the bracket [A,B] and evaluate it against G; the bracket is not in the span, so no regular level set can be tangent to the distribution.

items.title: Scope of point symmetries: symmetries belong to the Lagrangian, not to the configuration space, and time translation is the energy case
items.design_state: completed-local-remark; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
- **The symmetry is a property of the Lagrangian.** The identity of
  [[def-cm-infinitesimal-point-symmetry]] involves both the kinetic part and the potential of
  $\mathcal L$; a transformation that is a symmetry of the configuration space, of a chart or of a
  kinematic structure need not leave a chosen $\mathcal L$ invariant. The corollary
  [[cor-cm-noether-charges-for-translations-rotations-and-boosts]] exhibits the failure
  explicitly: for the confining potential $U(q)=\tfrac k2|q|^2$ the translation and boost
  identities fail even though the Galilean charts of the framework remain available. A symmetry
  hypothesis must therefore be verified for the actual model before
  [[thm-cm-point-symmetry-charge-is-conserved]] or
  [[thm-cm-point-noether-identity-with-time-reparametrization]] can be applied.

- **Time translation is a separate case.** The general theorem includes the case
  $\xi=0,\tau=1,B=0$, where the charge is the energy $-E$ and the identity holds exactly when
  $\mathcal L_t=0$; this agrees with the energy identity of
  [[prop-cm-hamiltonian-branch-identities]] in the autonomous case. Time-dependent Lagrangians
  need not conserve energy, and no conservation is claimed when $\mathcal L_t\ne0$.

- **Conservation is conditional and model-internal.** The conserved charges are deductions from
  the stated symmetry identities along solutions of the Euler–Lagrange equation. Nothing here
  asserts that an observed conservation law implies a symmetry of a physical model, or that the
  models possessing these symmetries describe nature; those are separate modelling and empirical
  questions, and the empirical qualifications of any such use belong to the consuming physical
  items.
items.strategy: Record the model-internal and conditional character of the conservation statements; no proof obligation.

items.title: Scope of stationarity: stationary is not minimum, and no second-variation theory is developed here
items.design_state: completed-local-remark; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
- Stationarity, as defined in [[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]] and characterised
  by [[thm-cm-stationarity-iff-euler-lagrange]], is the vanishing of the first variation for all
  fixed-endpoint variations. It is *not* the statement that $q$ minimizes the action, nor that it
  is a local minimum. The companion page exhibits an explicit quadratic model in which a stationary
  curve is not a local minimum: for the Lagrangian $\mathcal L(q,v)=\tfrac12(v^2-4q^2)$ on
  $[0,\pi]$ and the stationary curve $q_*(t)=\sin 2t$, the exact identity
  $S(q_*+\epsilon\sin)-S(q_*)=-\tfrac{3\pi}{4}\epsilon^2$ shows that every nearby element of the
  one-parameter family has strictly smaller action.

- No second variation, and no convexity or coercivity hypothesis, is introduced on this page. The
  stationarity theorem is an equivalence between zero first variation and the Euler–Lagrange equation. For a local extremum on fixed-endpoint $C^2$ curves, use the norm $\|q\|_{C^2}:=\max_{0\le j\le2}\sup_{t\in[a,b]}\|q^{(j)}(t)\|_2$. Each admissible family $q+s\eta$ tends to $q$ in this norm; a local extremum therefore gives an extremum at $s=0$ of its differentiable action, whose derivative is zero. Thus the Euler–Lagrange equation is necessary for such extrema, while stationarity alone need not give an extremum.

- The finite-interval chart statements on this page concern $C^2$ data and a fixed interval
  $[a,b]$. They make no claim about minimizers in a Sobolev or absolutely continuous class, about
  broken extremals, or about boundary conditions other than fixed endpoints; those belong to the
  calculus-of-variations development of the mathematical library.
items.strategy: Record the exact content and the exclusions of the stationarity notion; no proof obligation.

items.title: Scope of the Legendre map: regular versus hyperregular, the meaning of the covector datum, and the limits of the branch description
items.design_state: completed-local-remark; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
- **Regularity is local; hyperregularity is global in the fibre.** The derivative criterion of
  [[lem-cm-legendre-map-local-invertibility]] produces inverse branches only near points where the
  velocity Hessian is nonsingular, whereas hyperregularity as defined in
  [[def-cm-legendre-map-in-a-time-dependent-chart]] demands a bijection of each velocity fibre
  onto the full momentum fibre with globally defined inverse. Hyperregularity implies regularity: differentiating the inverse fibre identity gives $D_pv\,\mathcal L_{vv}=I_n$, hence a nonsingular Hessian. Regularity does not imply hyperregularity, as the bounded-gradient example shows; and the propositions on this page state explicitly which hypothesis each
  conclusion uses: the differential and energy identities
  [[prop-cm-hamiltonian-branch-identities]] use a branch, and the elimination in
  [[thm-cm-hamilton-phase-action-stationarity]] uses a global branch for the chart.

- **The mechanical chart is the positive example.** For
  $\mathcal L(t,q,v)=\tfrac12v^{\mathsf T}G(t,q)v+A(t,q)\cdot v-V(t,q)$ with $G$ symmetric
  positive definite, [[prop-cm-mechanical-chart-lagrangian-is-hyperregular]] proves
  hyperregularity and computes the Hamiltonian explicitly. The companion page records the
  degenerate cases: a regular Lagrangian whose velocity gradient is not onto the momentum fibre is
  not hyperregular, and the identically zero Lagrangian is not even regular, so it admits no
  Legendre inverse at all.

- **The covector datum $A$ and the momentum.** In the mechanical chart the momentum is
  $p=Gv+A$; it is a covector determined by the chart data, not $\text{mass}\times\text{velocity}$
  unless $G$ is a constant scalar matrix and $A=0$. The datum $A$ is a mathematical field on the
  chart and is not, in this development, an electromagnetic potential; identifying $A$ with a
  physical vector potential is a modelling step belonging to the consuming physics items, and
  requires its own assumptions and units.

- **No completeness or global solvability is asserted.** The branch description of the motion is
  local in the momentum variable and requires the invertibility hypotheses above. It does not
  assert that the Euler–Lagrange or Hamilton equations have global solutions, and the finite-time
  breakdown of a solution is not excluded by anything on this page.
items.strategy: Record the local/global distinction with its witnesses and the scope of the covector datum; no proof obligation.

items.title: The endpoint action function of a smooth family of extremals has differential $dW=p\,dq-H\,dt$
items.design_state: completed-local-theorem; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ and $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and nonempty, and let
$\mathcal L:J\times U\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be a fibre-full $C^2$ time-dependent
Lagrangian chart that is hyperregular, with inverse Legendre branch $v$ and Hamiltonian
$H(t,q,p)=p\cdot v(t,q,p)-\mathcal L(t,q,v(t,q,p))$
([[def-cm-legendre-map-in-a-time-dependent-chart]],
[[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]]). Fix $t_0\in J$ and $q_0\in U$, let $T\subseteq J\setminus\{t_0\}$ be open and nonempty, and let
$Q\subseteq U$ be open and nonempty, let $D\subseteq T\times Q\times J$ be open, and let
$X:D\to U$ be a $C^2$ map such that for every $(t,q)\in T\times Q$ the points $(t,q,t)$ and
$(t,q,t_0)$ lie in $D$, the closed interval with endpoints $t_0$ and $t$ is contained in the
$s$-section $D_{t,q}:=\{s\in J:(t,q,s)\in D\}$, which is required to be an open interval, and:

1. $X(t,q,t)=q$ and $X(t,q,t_0)=q_0$;
2. $s\mapsto X(t,q,s)$ is a solution of the Euler–Lagrange equation of $\mathcal L$ on the open
   interval $D_{t,q}$, i.e. $\bigl(s,X(t,q,s),\partial_sX(t,q,s)\bigr)\in J\times U\times\mathbb R^n$
   and $E_{\mathcal L}\bigl(X(t,q,\cdot)\bigr)=0$ on $D_{t,q}$.

Define

$$p(t,q):=\mathcal L_v\bigl(t,q,\partial_sX(t,q,t)\bigr),\qquad W(t,q):=\int_{t_0}^{t}\mathcal L\bigl(s,X(t,q,s),\partial_sX(t,q,s)\bigr)ds\qquad\bigl((t,q)\in T\times Q\bigr).$$

Then $W$ is of class $C^1$ on $T\times Q$ and

$$W_q(t,q)=p(t,q),\qquad W_t(t,q)=-H\bigl(t,q,p(t,q)\bigr)\qquad\bigl((t,q)\in T\times Q\bigr).$$
items.strategy: Differentiate the endpoint integral in q and t; integration by parts and the Euler-Lagrange equation cancel the interior terms, and the endpoint identities give W_q=p and W_t=-H.

items.title: Stationarity of the phase-space action is equivalent to Hamilton's equations, and hyperregular elimination recovers the Lagrangian action
items.design_state: completed-local-theorem; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $O_H\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n$ be open and nonempty,
let $H:O_H\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$, let $a<b$, and suppose that for a $C^1$ path
$\gamma(t)=(q(t),p(t))$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]],
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]) with $(t,q(t),p(t))\in O_H$ for all $t\in[a,b]$
the **phase action**

$$A(\gamma):=\int_a^b\bigl[p(t)\cdot q'(t)-H(t,q(t),p(t))\bigr]dt$$

is defined, the integrand being continuous ([[def-darboux-integral]],
[[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then:

1. for every $C^1$ variation pair $(\delta q,\delta p)$ with $\delta q(a)=\delta q(b)=0$ and with
   $\gamma+s(\delta q,\delta p)$ in the domain of $A$ for small $|s|$,

$$\frac{d}{ds}\Big|_{s=0}A\bigl(\gamma+s(\delta q,\delta p)\bigr) =\int_a^b\Bigl[\bigl(q'-H_p\bigr)\cdot\delta p+\bigl(-p'-H_q\bigr)\cdot\delta q\Bigr]dt ;$$

2. $\gamma$ is **stationary** (the displayed derivative vanishes for every such variation) if and
   only if Hamilton's equations hold on $[a,b]$:

$$q'(t)=H_p\bigl(t,q(t),p(t)\bigr),\qquad p'(t)=-H_q\bigl(t,q(t),p(t)\bigr)\qquad(t\in[a,b]);$$

3. **(elimination)** let in addition $\mathcal L:J\times U\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be a
   hyperregular $C^2$ chart with inverse branch $v(t,q,p)$ and Hamiltonian
   $H(t,q,p)=p\cdot v(t,q,p)-\mathcal L(t,q,v(t,q,p))$
   ([[def-cm-legendre-map-in-a-time-dependent-chart]]), such that the phase domain of $H$ contains
   the points below. For every $C^2$ curve $q:[a,b]\to U$ with $(t,q(t),q'(t))$ in the domain of
   $\mathcal L$, put $p(t):=\mathcal L_v(t,q(t),q'(t))$. Then
   $A(q,p)=S(q)$, where $S$ is the action of $\mathcal L$; consequently $q$ is stationary for $S$
   if and only if $(q,p)$ is stationary for the phase action.
items.strategy: Integrate by parts to remove the interior endpoints of p; a bump argument per component identifies the Hamilton equations as exactly the vanishing coefficient conditions.

items.title: Noether identity for point transformations with time reparametrisation: the conserved charge $p\cdot\xi-E\tau-B$
items.design_state: completed-local-theorem; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
Let $(O,\mathcal L)$ be a time-dependent Lagrangian chart over $[a,b]\times U$
([[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]]). Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open and contain the time-configuration projection of $O$. Let
$\tau,\xi:A\to\mathbb R,\mathbb R^n$ and
$B:A\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$, and for a $C^1$ function
$\varphi(t,q)$ with scalar values write $D_t\varphi(t,q,v):=\varphi_t(t,q)+\varphi_q(t,q)\cdot v$; for vector-valued $\xi$ set $D_t\xi:=\xi_t+D_q\xi\,v$, equivalently $(D_t\xi)_j=D_t(\xi_j)$. Assume the
**Noether identity**

$$\mathcal L_t\,\tau+\mathcal L_q\cdot\xi+\mathcal L_v\cdot\bigl(D_t\xi-v\,D_t\tau\bigr) +\mathcal L\,D_t\tau=D_tB$$

on $O$, where all arguments of $\mathcal L$ and its derivatives are $(t,q,v)$. Write $p:=\mathcal L_v$ for the momentum and put

$$E(t,q,v):=\mathcal L_v(t,q,v)\cdot v-\mathcal L(t,q,v),\qquad C(t,q,v):=\mathcal L_v(t,q,v)\cdot\xi(t,q)-E(t,q,v)\tau(t,q)-B(t,q).$$

Then for every $C^2$ curve $q:I\to U$ on an open interval $I\supseteq[a,b]$ with
$(t,q(t),q'(t))\in O$ that solves the Euler–Lagrange equation
$E_{\mathcal L}(q)(t)=0$, the function $t\mapsto C(t,q(t),q'(t))$ is constant on $I$.
Moreover:

1. at $\tau=0$ and with $\xi$ independent of $t$ the Noether identity is exactly the infinitesimal point symmetry identity of
   [[def-cm-infinitesimal-point-symmetry]] for the pair $(\xi,B)$, and the charge reduces to
   $C=\mathcal L_v\cdot\xi-B$, so the present theorem specialises to
   [[thm-cm-point-symmetry-charge-is-conserved]];
2. at $\xi=0$, $\tau=1$, $B=0$ the Noether identity holds if and only if $\mathcal L_t=0$ on $O$,
   and the charge is $C=-E$; thus the theorem contains the conservation of the energy in the
   time-independent case, in agreement with clause 3 of
   [[prop-cm-hamiltonian-branch-identities]].
items.strategy: Differentiate the charge along an Euler-Lagrange solution; the identity is exactly the vanishing condition.

items.design_state: completed-local-example; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
Let $n=1$, $[a,b]=[0,\pi]$, $U=\mathbb R$, and
$\mathcal L(q,v)=\tfrac12\bigl(v^2-4q^2\bigr)$, a $C^\infty$ (hence $C^2$) Lagrangian on
$\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R$ ([[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]],
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Let

$$q_*(t):=\sin 2t,\qquad \eta(t):=\sin t .$$

Use fixed-endpoint admissible $C^2$ curves with $q(0)=q(\pi)=0$ and the norm $\|q\|_{C^2}:=\max_{0\le j\le2}\sup_{t\in[0,\pi]}|q^{(j)}(t)|$. A local minimum means $S(q_*)\le S(q)$ for all admissible $q$ in some ball about $q_*$ in this norm. Then $q_*$ is a stationary curve of the action
$S(q)=\int_0^\pi\tfrac12(q'^2-4q^2)dt$, and for the one-parameter family
$q_*+\epsilon\eta$ one has the exact identity

$$S(q_*+\epsilon\eta)=S(q_*)-\frac{3\pi}{4}\epsilon^2\qquad(\epsilon\in\mathbb R).$$

In particular $S(q_*+\epsilon\eta)<S(q_*)$ for every $\epsilon\ne0$: the stationary curve is not a
local minimum of the action. The model has no minimiser at all, since
$S(\lambda\eta)=-\tfrac{3\pi}{4}\lambda^2\to-\infty$ as $|\lambda|\to\infty$.

items.title: Regular versus hyperregular: the bounded-gradient Lagrangian $\sqrt{1+v^2}$ and the degenerate zero Lagrangian
items.design_state: completed-local-example; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
Take $n=1$, $J=U=\mathbb R$, and consider the three fibre-full $C^2$ Lagrangians
$\mathcal L_1(v)=\sqrt{1+v^2}$, $\mathcal L_2(v)=0$ and $\mathcal L_3(v)=\tfrac12v^2$ on
$J\times U\times\mathbb R$ ([[def-cm-legendre-map-in-a-time-dependent-chart]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal L_1$ is regular on the chart but **not** hyperregular: its velocity Hessian is
   $(1+v^2)^{-3/2}>0$ at every $v$, while the fibre Legendre map
   $v\mapsto\mathcal L_1'(v)=v/\sqrt{1+v^2}$ has range $(-1,1)$, so it is not surjective onto
   $\mathbb R$;
2. $\mathcal L_2$ is neither regular nor hyperregular: $\mathcal L_2'\equiv0$ and
   $\mathcal L_2''\equiv0$, so the velocity Hessian is singular everywhere and the fibre map is
   constant, hence not injective;
3. $\mathcal L_3$ is both regular and hyperregular: $\mathcal L_3''\equiv1$ and the fibre map
   $v\mapsto v$ is a $C^\infty$ bijection of $\mathbb R$ onto itself.

Thus regularity does not imply hyperregularity, and neither condition is automatic.
items.strategy: Compute the derivatives and ranges of the three fibre maps and compare with the definitions of regularity and hyperregularity.

items.title: The ideal planar pendulum: equation of motion, conserved energy, Lyapunov stability and the frequency $\sqrt{g/l}$
items.design_state: completed-local-example; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
Let $m,l,g>0$ and let $\Omega:=(-\pi,\pi)\subseteq\mathbb R$. Consider the embedding

$$X:\Omega\to\mathbb R^2,\qquad X(\theta):=\bigl(l\sin\theta,\,-l\cos\theta\bigr),$$

the ambient mass $M:=mI_2$ and the constant force $F:=(0,-mg)$. Let $\theta:I\to\Omega$ be a
$C^2$ curve and put $x(t):=X(\theta(t))$. Then:

1. $X$ is a $C^3$ immersion with $\|X'(\theta)\|_2=l$ for every $\theta$; if the ambient motion
   satisfies $Mx''=F+R$ with $R(t)\cdot X'(\theta(t))\delta=0$ for all $\delta\in\mathbb R$, then

$$ml^2\theta''(t)+mgl\sin\theta(t)=0\qquad(t\in I);$$

2. the **reduced energy** $E(\theta,\theta'):=\tfrac12ml^2\theta'^2-mgl\cos\theta$ is constant
   along every solution of the equation;
3. $\theta=0$ is a strict local minimum of the reduced potential
   $U_{\mathrm{red}}(\theta):=-mgl\cos\theta$ on $\Omega$, and the equilibrium $(0,0)$ of the
   pendulum system $\theta'=v$, $v'=-(g/l)\sin\theta$ is Lyapunov stable;
4. the linearisation at $\theta=0$ is $ml^2\xi''+mgl\xi=0$, a quadratic mode with angular
   frequency

$$\omega=\sqrt{g/l}.$$

items.title: The rotating hoop: reduced Lagrangian, the equation $\theta''=\Omega^2\sin\theta\cos\theta-(g/a)\sin\theta$, and the reduced energy versus the inertial mechanical energy
items.design_state: completed-local-example; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
Let $a,m,g>0$ and $\Omega\in\mathbb R$, and let

$$X:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3,\qquad X(\theta,t):=\bigl(a\sin\theta\cos(\Omega t),\,a\sin\theta\sin(\Omega t),\,a(1-\cos\theta)\bigr),$$

the position of a point of a circle of radius $a$ rotating about the vertical axis with constant
angular speed $\Omega$. For an open interval $I$ and a $C^2$ curve
$\theta:I\to\mathbb R$ put $x(t):=X(\theta(t),t)$. Stationarity on $I$ means stationarity of the restricted curve on every $[t_1,t_2]\subseteq I$ with $t_1<t_2$, using fixed-endpoint variations. Then:

1. $\dot x=X_\theta\theta'+X_t$ and $\frac12m|\dot x|^2=\frac12ma^2\bigl(\theta'^2+\Omega^2\sin^2\theta\bigr)$,
   while $\ddot x\cdot X_\theta=a^2\theta''-a^2\Omega^2\sin\theta\cos\theta$;
2. the curves $\theta$ that are stationary for the action of the time-dependent Lagrangian chart
   $L(\theta,v):=\frac12ma^2\bigl(v^2+\Omega^2\sin^2\theta\bigr)-mga(1-\cos\theta)$ on
   $O:=\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R$ are exactly the $C^2$ solutions of

$$\theta''=\Omega^2\sin\theta\cos\theta-\frac{g}{a}\sin\theta ;$$

3. the **reduced energy** $E(\theta,v):=\frac12ma^2v^2-\frac12ma^2\Omega^2\sin^2\theta-mga\cos\theta$
   is constant along every $C^2$ solution, whereas the inertial kinetic-plus-potential energy
   $K+U_g=\frac12m|\dot x|^2+mga(1-\cos\theta)$ satisfies

$$\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(K+U_g\bigr)=2ma^2\Omega^2\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\theta'=ma^2\Omega^2\frac{d}{dt}\sin^2\theta$$

   along every solution, and equals $E+ma^2\Omega^2\sin^2\theta+mga$; it is therefore in general
   not conserved, and it differs from $E$ by $ma^2\Omega^2\sin^2\theta+mga$;
4. if the ambient motion is additionally modelled by $m\ddot x=(0,0,-mg)+R$ with an ideal
   reaction satisfying $R(t)\cdot X_\theta(\theta(t),t)=0$, then the same equation of part 2 holds,
   and the reaction power is

$$R\cdot\dot x=\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(K+U_g\bigr)=2ma^2\Omega^2\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\theta' ,$$

   generally nonzero: the prescribed rotation can do work on the point;
5. if $a\Omega^2\le g$, then $0$ is a strict local minimum of
   $U_{\mathrm{eff}}(\theta):=-\frac12ma^2\Omega^2\sin^2\theta-mga\cos\theta$ with
   $U_{\mathrm{eff}}'(0)=0$, and the equilibrium $(0,0)$ of
   $\theta'=v,\ v'=\Omega^2\sin\theta\cos\theta-(g/a)\sin\theta$ is Lyapunov stable; if
   $a\Omega^2>g$, then $0$ is not a local minimum of $U_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and the stability
   criterion does not apply.
items.strategy: Compute the carrier kinematics, identify the reduced Lagrangian and its Euler-Lagrange equation, differentiate the two energies along solutions, and contract the ambient equation with the tangent for the reaction power.

items.title: The planar rolling disk: the holonomic constraint $x-a\theta=\mathrm{const}$ and the acceleration $f/(m+I/a^{2})$
items.design_state: completed-local-example; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
Let $a,m,I>0$ and $f\in\mathbb R$, and consider the two-coordinate model

$$\mathcal G(x,\theta):=x-a\theta,\qquad M:=\begin{pmatrix}m&0\\0&I\end{pmatrix},\qquad \Phi:=(f,0),$$

on $O:=\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^2$, where $x$ is a centre coordinate and $\theta$ an oriented spin.
The constraint $\mathcal G=0$ is the ideal planar no-slip law of a disk of radius $a$ rolling in a
straight line; $M$ is the adopted kinetic matrix (mass $m$, spin inertia $I$), and $\Phi$ the
adopted applied force (force $f$ along $x$, zero spin torque). Then:

1. $\mathcal G$ is a regular holonomic constraint: $\mathcal G_q=(1,-a)$ has rank one and its
   kernel is the line $\mathbb R(a,1)$ of virtual displacements. The associated differential
   constraint $x'-a\theta'=0$ is exact: on an interval it holds exactly when $x-a\theta$ is
   constant, so in this planar straight-line case the rolling law is holonomic, and after
   translating $x$ the constant may be taken to be $0$;
2. if $q=(x,\theta):J\to\mathbb R^2$ is a $C^2$ ideal-constraint motion of
   $(\mathcal G,M,\Phi)$ ([[def-cm-holonomic-constraint-and-ideal-reactions]]), then the
   d'Alembert condition gives $\bigl(mx''-f\bigr)a+I\theta''=0$, and differentiating the
   constraint twice gives $x''=a\theta''$; hence

$$\Bigl(m+\frac{I}{a^2}\Bigr)x''=f,\qquad x''=\frac{fa^2}{I+ma^2},\qquad \theta''=\frac{af}{I+ma^2};$$

3. the multiplier of the motion is $\lambda=-\dfrac{fI}{I+ma^{2}}$ (uniquely determined), the
   reaction is $R=\mathcal G_q^{\mathsf T}\lambda=(\lambda,-a\lambda)$ with $|\lambda|=|f|\dfrac{I}{I+ma^2}\le|f|$, with strict inequality exactly when $f\ne0$,
   and the proposition [[prop-cm-ideal-holonomic-system-in-a-time-dependent-chart]] reproduces
   these numbers from $C=\mathcal G_qM^{-1}\mathcal G_q^{\mathsf T}=\frac1m+\frac{a^2}{I}$ and
   $\Lambda=-C^{-1}\mathcal G_qM^{-1}\Phi$;
4. for a uniform thin disk, $I=\frac12ma^2$ and $x''=\frac{2f}{3m}$; for a hoop (all mass at the
   rim), $I=ma^2$ and $x''=\frac{f}{2m}$;
5. the quadratic motion
   $x(t)=x_0+v_0t+\frac{fa^2t^2}{2(I+ma^2)}$, $\theta(t)=\theta_0+\omega_0t+\frac{aft^2}{2(I+ma^2)}$
   with $x_0=a\theta_0$ and $v_0=a\omega_0$ is an ideal-constraint motion with constant multiplier
   $\lambda$, so the computed acceleration is realised by an explicit solution.
items.strategy: Project the ideal equation onto the virtual displacement, differentiate the constraint twice, solve the linear system, and realise the motion explicitly.
